title: Retry schedule
topic: Pushing arrow functions that capture `i` inside a JS `for` loop
blurb: A JS helper that builds per-attempt retry callbacks in a loop.
prompt: Spec: for `steps = 3`, return 3 zero-arg functions returning `{ attempt: 1, delayMs: 200 }` through `{ attempt: 3, delayMs: 600 }`. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.
conclusion: AI summary: Each returned function keeps its own `attempt` (1..steps) and `delayMs` (200..steps*200).

diagnosis: Missing `async` keyword means `delayMs` never pauses execution when callbacks run.
If `steps` is `0`, JavaScript throws a RangeError without an early guard.
Function declarations aren't hoisted when they return arrow functions.
`steps` should default to `1` or `for` loops silently execute once.
fix: Mark the function `async function makeRetryPlan(steps)`.
Add `if (steps <= 0) return [];` at the top.
Rewrite as `const makeRetryPlan = (steps = 1) => ...`.
Convert `steps` with `Math.max(1, steps)`.

diagnosis: Declaring `const tasks = []` freezes the array, so `tasks.push(...)` throws TypeError.
Using `const` inside a function shares one `tasks` array across calls.
`tasks` must be declared with `let` before pushing closures into it.
Creating `tasks` before the loop causes every closure to share the same scope.
fix: Change `const tasks = []` to `let tasks = []` so `.push()` is allowed.
Use `new Array(steps)` instead of `[]` so indices match.
Move `const tasks = []` inside the `for` loop.
Return `tasks.slice()` on line 7 to avoid sharing.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `i < steps` stops at `steps - 1`, so `steps = 3` only creates 2 tasks.
Using `i++` increments `i` before `delayMs` is computed on the first iteration.
Looping from `0` makes the first `attempt` equal `0` instead of `1`.
`let i` is hoisted to the function top in JavaScript, so all closures share the final value of `i`.
fix: Change `i < steps` to `i <= steps` so the last retry isn't dropped.
Start at `for (let i = 1; i <= steps; i++)` to avoid off-by-one attempts.
Wrap the loop body in an IIFE `(function(n) { ... })(i)` so `i` isn't shared.
Replace `i++` with `++i` so the step counter advances cleanly.

diagnosis: Declaring `const delayMs` inside a loop throws SyntaxError on the second iteration because `const` cannot be reassigned.
`(i + 1) * 200` produces `200, 400, 600` only if `i` starts at 1; starting at 0 gives `0, 200, 400`.
`delayMs` is overwritten on every iteration, so every closure reads the final `600`.
Operator precedence computes `1 * 200` before adding `i`, giving `200, 201, 202`.
fix: Change `const delayMs` to `let delayMs` declared before the `for` loop.
Multiply `i * 200` instead of `(i + 1) * 200`.
Inline `(i + 1) * 200` inside the object literal instead of using `const`.
Add extra parentheses `((i + 1) * 200)` to fix precedence.

diagnosis: Closure trap: every pushed arrow function captures the same loop variable `i`, so calling any of them returns `{ attempt: 4, delayMs: 600 }`.
Arrow function `() => ({ ... })` treats `{ ... }` as a block body instead of an object literal, returning `undefined`.
Object shorthand `delayMs` inside the arrow function references `undefined` once the loop exits.
`tasks.push` immediately invokes the arrow function instead of storing a callable task.
fix: Wrap the push in an IIFE `((idx) => tasks.push(() => ...))(i)` so each closure gets its own `i`.
Replace `() => ({ ... })` with `() => { return { attempt: i + 1, delayMs }; }`.
Copy `const attempt = i + 1` and return `Object.freeze({ attempt, delayMs })`.
Use `tasks[i] = ...` instead of `tasks.push(...)` so the closure binds early.

diagnosis: Missing semicolon after the `for` block causes JS automatic semicolon insertion to break `return`.
Exiting the loop destroys `delayMs` before the closures can read it.
The closing brace terminates `makeRetryPlan` early, making `return tasks` unreachable.
Leaving the loop leaves `i` equal to `steps`, overwriting all saved `attempt` values.
fix: Add a semicolon `};` after the `for` loop.
Save `delayMs` on `this.delayMs` so it survives the block exit.
Move `return tasks;` inside the loop before the closing brace.
Snapshot `i` with `tasks.map` after the loop instead.

diagnosis: Returning `tasks` returns functions instead of `{ attempt, delayMs }` objects.
Returning `tasks` before calling each function means `delayMs` is never evaluated.
`tasks` is out of scope here because it was mutated inside the loop.
Returning `tasks` directly returns a shared array if `makeRetryPlan` is called twice.
fix: Return `tasks.map(fn => fn())` so callers get the objects directly.
Return `[...tasks]` so callers get a fresh array copy.
Return `Object.freeze(tasks)` to lock in the closure values.
Call `tasks.reverse()` before returning so attempt 1 runs first.

diagnosis: Missing `module.exports` makes `makeRetryPlan` impossible to call.
Closing the function without freeing `i` leaks `i` onto the global object.
JavaScript requires `return;` at the end of functions that build closures.
Unclosed parenthesis on line 5 causes a syntax error at the closing brace.
fix: Add `export default makeRetryPlan;` after the closing brace.
Add `i = 0;` before the closing brace to prevent a global leak.
Check the parentheses around `({ attempt: i + 1, delayMs })`.
Wrap the whole function in `'use strict';`.

clean_conclusion: The closure-in-a-loop bug only bites with `var`. In JS, `for (let i = ...)` creates a fresh binding for `i` on every iteration, so each callback keeps its own `attempt` (1, 2, 3) and `delayMs` (200, 400, 600).
explanation: The closure-in-a-loop bug only bites with `var`. In JS, `for (let i = ...)` creates a fresh binding for `i` on every iteration, so each callback keeps its own `attempt` (1, 2, 3) and `delayMs` (200, 400, 600).
